table.text: All participants previously completed a lab-based study (IRB# 90369) examining emotional learning and exercise in PTSD and agreed to be contacted about additional research.
This study was approved by the University of Kentucky Non-Medical Institutional Review Board (IRB# 101765) and preregistered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07080606).
After providing IRB-approved informed consent, participants completed a battery of questionnaires, and a clinician administered psychodiagnostic interview to evaluate inclusion/exclusion criteria.

Participants were included in the study if they could ethically provide informed consent, were aged 18-64, could safely engage in 25 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, and met DSM-5 criteria for PTSD within the past month.
Participants were excluded if they were currently undergoing PTSD psychotherapy or had recent changes in psychiatric medication or psychotherapy (i.e., < 4 weeks).
table.formatted: Participants were excluded if they were currently undergoing PTSD psychotherapy or had recent changes in psychiatric medication or psychotherapy (i.e., < 4 weeks).

table.text: Participants were invited to complete a prescreening form via REDCap.
Fifteen volunteers were prescreened; twelve were invited to participate.
Three participants were deemed ineligible as they did not meet the DSM-5 criteria for PTSD during the psychodiagnostic interview.
After providing IRB-approved informed consent, participants completed a battery of questionnaires, and a clinician administered psychodiagnostic interview to evaluate inclusion/exclusion criteria.
Eligible participants were randomized (1:1:1) to a three-, four-, or five-week baseline period.
After the baseline assessment phase, participants completed eight sessions of BET, including six sessions of imaginal exposure to traumatic memories followed by moderate-intensity aerobic exercise.
During the last treatment session, participants were asked to provide satisfaction ratings and qualitative feedback during a semi-structured interview.

Participants completed four weeks of follow-up questionnaires after treatment, resulting in a total of 11-13 weeks of repeated self-report assessments across the baseline, treatment, and follow-up phases.
Participants were asked to report pre-, post-, and peak subjective units of distress (SUDs) across all exposure sessions, a commonly used measure in exposure therapy (Wolpe & Lazarus, 1966).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

ethics_statements: All participants previously completed a lab-based study (IRB# 90369) examining emotional learning and exercise in PTSD and agreed to be contacted about additional research.
This study was approved by the University of Kentucky Non-Medical Institutional Review Board (IRB# 101765) and preregistered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07080606).
After providing IRB-approved informed consent, participants completed a battery of questionnaires, and a clinician administered psychodiagnostic interview to evaluate inclusion/exclusion criteria.
live_data_statements: Participants were included in the study if they could ethically provide informed consent, were aged 18-64, could safely engage in 25 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, and met DSM-5 criteria for PTSD within the past month.
Participants were excluded if they were currently undergoing PTSD psychotherapy or had recent changes in psychiatric medication or psychotherapy (i.e., < 4 weeks).
Participants were invited to complete a prescreening form via REDCap.
Fifteen volunteers were prescreened; twelve were invited to participate.
Three participants were deemed ineligible as they did not meet the DSM-5 criteria for PTSD during the psychodiagnostic interview.
After providing IRB-approved informed consent, participants completed a battery of questionnaires, and a clinician administered psychodiagnostic interview to evaluate inclusion/exclusion criteria.
Eligible participants were randomized (1:1:1) to a three-, four-, or five-week baseline period.
After the baseline assessment phase, participants completed eight sessions of BET, including six sessions of imaginal exposure to traumatic memories followed by moderate-intensity aerobic exercise.
During the last treatment session, participants were asked to provide satisfaction ratings and qualitative feedback during a semi-structured interview.

Participants completed four weeks of follow-up questionnaires after treatment, resulting in a total of 11-13 weeks of repeated self-report assessments across the baseline, treatment, and follow-up phases.
Participants were asked to report pre-, post-, and peak subjective units of distress (SUDs) across all exposure sessions, a commonly used measure in exposure therapy (Wolpe & Lazarus, 1966).

Before and after exposures, participants were asked to evaluate the likelihood of their negative expectations about the exposure to facilitate expectancy violations (Craske et al., 2008; Kooistra et al., 2025).

Instead of using out-of-session homework between exposures, participants were instructed to practice allowing themselves to experience thoughts, images, or feelings that arise between sessions, similarly to the instructions used in written exposure therapy (Sloan & Marx, 2019).
During the warm-up, participants had 3 minutes to reach the target heart rate.
Participants were instructed to adjust their heart rate to stay within their 70-75% MHR range.

Weekly scores of outcome variables for each participant are graphically plotted to compare levels (i.e., mean scores) between phases, trends (i.e., slopes) of scores within each phase, variability of scores within each phase, immediacy of the treatment's effect, consistency of effects between subjects, and overlap of data between phases (Lane & Gast, 2014; Ledford et al., 2018).
Following their intake, participants completed the CEQ to assess the credibility and initial expectations of the BET and exercise protocol.
Participants provided qualitative feedback about the acceptability and feasibility of the BET and exercise treatment during the treatment feedback interview.
Four participants (P1, P3, P4, and P6) exhibited large non-overlap (Tau-U Range = -.80 to -.100) for PTSD symptom severity scores between baseline and treatment phases.
All participants from the current study were recruited following completion of another study investigating neural mechanisms in emotional learning and exercise in PTSD among adults exposed to IPV.
The current sample was relatively homogenous and may not generalize to other populations as participants were all white females with IPV-related trauma.

Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is associated with an increased risk of multiple physical (e.g., cardiovascular and metabolic) and mental (e.g., depression and substance use) health conditions (Asnaani et al., 2014; Pietrzak et al., 2012; Qassem et al., 2021), including an increased risk of non-suicidal self-injury, suicide attempts, and death by suicide (Alharbi et al., 2020; Forehand et al., 2022).

text.text: Exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapies (CBT), such as prolonged exposure (PE), are gold-standard psychosocial treatments for PTSD (Foa et al., 2007; Rauch et al., 2012).

text.text: Exposurebased treatments help patients safely process their traumatic experience(s), learn how to tolerate distressing emotions and trauma reminders, and overcome maladaptive internal and external avoidance behaviors (Foa et al., 2007).

text.text: Unfortunately, approximately a quarter of patients prematurely drop out of PE (22-28%; Varker et al., 2021), response rates are modest (53-60%; Schnurr et al., 2007), and significant relapse of symptoms is common (57%; Brooks & Greenberg, 2024).

text.text: It is crucial to develop and implement strategies that improve exposure-based treatments for PTSD.

Fear extinction processes are important mechanisms of exposure therapies, as the formation and consolidation of new safety learning inhibits conditioned fear responses and associated reactivity to trauma cues when safety learning memories are effectively recalled (Craske et al., 2008; Fullana et al., 2020).

text.text: Through repeated imaginal and in vivo exposures, individuals learn to more effectively distinguish threat and safety cues across contexts (e.g., environments and interoceptive states) and to more appropriately recall learned inhibitory safety memories (Maren et al., 2013).

text.text: Changes in experiential and emotional avoidance are putative safety learning mechanisms, such that an increased willingness to engage with emotions during exposures may reduce subsequent maladaptive avoidance of negative emotions, posttraumatic intrusions, and reminders of trauma (Wang et al., 2024).

text.text: Methods for improving the consolidation of safety learning may be a promising augmentation strategy for exposure-based treatments to reduce unwanted return of fear.

Aerobic exercise is associated with several mental and physical health benefits and has well-established neurocognitive, neuroplastic, and neuromodulatory effects that improve safety learning memory consolidation (Azar et al., 2024; Crombie et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Aerobic exercise is associated with several mental and physical health benefits and has well-established neurocognitive, neuroplastic, and neuromodulatory effects that improve safety learning memory consolidation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Azar et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Crombie et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Animal studies using acute exercise during or after fear extinction report large improvements in fear extinction consolidation, as evidenced by reduced fear expression (i.e., freezing) during return of fear testing up to a week later (Tanner et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Animal studies using acute exercise during or after fear extinction report large improvements in fear extinction consolidation, as evidenced by reduced fear expression (i.e., freezing) during return of fear testing up to a week later <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Tanner et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Animal studies collectively indicate that exercise following safety learning could serve as an augmentation strategy for exposure therapy to enhance the strength and retention of safetylearning consolidation.

Attempts to translate preclinical findings of exercise and fear extinction or exposure therapy into human models have yielded mixed results, primarily due to methodological inconsistencies and limitations.

Most human studies that have attempted to use exercise prior to or separate from exposure/fear extinction have reported null or temporary improvements in clinical, fear extinction, or return of fear outcomes (Bischoff et al., 2018; Jacquart et al., 2017; Voorendonk et al., 2021; Weisman & Rodebaugh, 2018), which is unsurprising given the animal literature showing null effects of exercise before extinction (Tanner et al., 2018).

text.text: Conversely, human studies that have examined exercise after exposure therapy or fear extinction, which is aligned with preclinical data, have yielded more promising results.

In a sample of healthy women, fear extinction training followed by aerobic exercise at 70-75% MHR reduced threat expectancy ratings for the unconditioned stimulus (shock) 24 hours later compared with the active control condition (40-50% MHR; Crombie et al., 2023).

text.text: A large-scale randomized controlled trial (RCT) examined changes in PTSD severity following nine weekly exposure-based CBT sessions, followed by 20 minutes of active stretching (control) or 10 minutes of exercise at 65-85% MHR on a high stepper (plus 5 minutes of warm-up and cool-down).

This study reported a moderate effect size (d = 0.60) for between-group differences in PTSD symptom severity at five-month follow-up, and suggests that exercise following CBT enhanced long-term retention of safety memories and/or attenuated the return of fear over time, consistent with laboratory research (Bryant et al., 2023).

These findings may have been due to ceiling effects from a large dose of psychotherapy, the choice of an eclectic therapy approach that targets several treatment mechanisms in addition to safety learning (e.g., cognitive reappraisal), or an insufficient dose of exercise (e.g., duration or intensity; Bryant et al., 2023).

text.text: The current study attempted to augment safety learning through isolating and targeting exposure therapy mechanisms in a twice-weekly treatment using adequately dosed exercise (70-75% MHR for 25 minutes) within the consolidation window (i.e., after exposures).

The BET protocol attempted to overcome the largest barrier to PTSD treatment (i.e., participant dropout) by using shorter exposures, twice-weekly sessions, and no homework, while also trying to improve treatment response and retention of treatment gains by targeting exposure therapy mechanisms.

Although neuroplasticity was not directly assessed, the combined protocol was designed with exercise timing and dosage hypothesized to promote neuroplasticity during the post-exposure consolidation window (Azar et al., 2024).

text.text: Single case experimental designs (SCEDs) are parsimonious research designs that are ideal for preliminary investigations of treatment mechanisms and the efficacy of interventions, as they use each subject as their own control, resulting in high internal validity and the ability to examine effect sizes within-and between-subjects (Barlow et al., 2008; Ledford & Gast, 2018).

text.text: SCED clinical trial methodology is increasingly popular for initially evaluating the efficacy and mechanistic engagement of PTSD interventions (Au et al., 2017; Kooistra et al., 2025).

text.text: The current study used a staggered baseline SCED in an open-label clinical trial to pilot the feasibility and acceptability of twice-weekly brief exposure therapy (BET) followed by exercise for adults with PTSD.

We hypothesized that the BET and exercise protocol would be feasibly administered, with all sessions having less than a 20% deviation from the protocol checklist, and that individuals would report BET and exercise as an acceptable means of PTSD treatment.

We also hypothesized that individuals who received the BET and exercise protocol would exhibit improvements in PTSD symptom severity, experiential avoidance, posttraumatic cognitions, and negative affect during treatment and follow-up relative to the baseline phase.

Participants were included in the study if they could ethically provide informed consent, were aged 18-64, could safely engage in 25 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, and met DSM-5 criteria for PTSD within the past month.
Participants were excluded if they were currently undergoing PTSD psychotherapy or had recent changes in psychiatric medication or psychotherapy (i.e., < 4 weeks).
text.formatted: Participants were excluded if they were currently undergoing PTSD psychotherapy or had recent changes in psychiatric medication or psychotherapy (i.e., < 4 weeks).

text.text: Psychiatric exclusionary criteria included recent (within the past 3 months) severe substance use disorder(s), high risk for suicide (i.e., plan and intent to die by suicide or recent suicide attempt), mania, or psychotic symptoms.
Exercise-related exclusion criteria consisted of reported health conditions (e.g., heart disease, leg injury, asthma) that were not medically stable or deemed potentially unsafe for exercise.
Study completers consisted of six White women with a mean age of 33.0 years (range = 22-45 years).
Although all individuals were diagnosed with PTSD as their principal diagnosis, four individuals (67%) also met diagnostic criteria for other co-occurring psychiatric disorders.
All participants previously completed a lab-based study (IRB# 90369) examining emotional learning and exercise in PTSD and agreed to be contacted about additional research.
Participants were invited to complete a prescreening form via REDCap.

Participants who screened positive for probable PTSD and a likely safe ability to exercise were able to schedule a virtual telehealth intake via Zoom with the master's level clinician (TH) to assess study eligibility.
Fifteen volunteers were prescreened; twelve were invited to participate.
Ten consented to participate in the present study and completed an intake.
Three participants were deemed ineligible as they did not meet the DSM-5 criteria for PTSD during the psychodiagnostic interview.
One eligible participant withdrew from the study after enrollment but before starting baseline assessments due to logistical issues.
The final sample consisted of six participants (n = 6).

text.text: This study was approved by the University of Kentucky Non-Medical Institutional Review Board (IRB# 101765) and preregistered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07080606).
The current pilot open-label, randomized baseline study aimed to characterize the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of the BET and exercise protocol.

We combined CONsolidated Standards Of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) and SCED guidelines for the development and reporting of the current SCED clinical trial (Butcher et al., 2022; Kratochwill et al., 2026).

text.text: After providing IRB-approved informed consent, participants completed a battery of questionnaires, and a clinician administered psychodiagnostic interview to evaluate inclusion/exclusion criteria.
Eligible participants were randomized (1:1:1) to a three-, four-, or five-week baseline period.
After the baseline assessment phase, participants completed eight sessions of BET, including six sessions of imaginal exposure to traumatic memories followed by moderate-intensity aerobic exercise.
During the last treatment session, participants were asked to provide satisfaction ratings and qualitative feedback during a semi-structured interview.

Participants completed four weeks of follow-up questionnaires after treatment, resulting in a total of 11-13 weeks of repeated self-report assessments across the baseline, treatment, and follow-up phases.

Self-report assessments were administered weekly via REDCap links sent the day before the first session of each week; However, many participants did not complete questionnaires prior to the first session of each week, but 100% of questionnaires were completed before the subsequent week of treatment.
Consequently, symptom change is reported by study week rather than by session number to ensure consistency across timepoints.
Demographics and Baseline Characteristics.
Age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, household income, marital status, medication usage, and occupational status were assessed with single-item self-report questions.
Acceptability of the treatment protocol was assessed using a pretreatment questionnaire, a post-treatment participant-rated treatment feedback survey, and a clinician-administered interview.

The Credibility and Expectations Questionnaire (CEQ; Devilly & Borkovec, 2000) is a 6-item questionnaire used to assess participants' initial thoughts about the credibility and expectations of a treatment before it begins.

text.text: Items were rated on a 9-point Likert scale ranging from1 = 'Not at All' to9 = 'Very.'
The percent improvement items were converted to a 1-9 linear scale aligned with the other 4 items on the CEQ.
The credibility and expectation subscale scores range from 3-36, with higher scores indicating greater perceived credibility and expectations of treatment.
A modified treatment satisfaction questionnaire was used to assess participants' perceptions of the BET and exercise treatment.

The treatment satisfaction questionnaire included 6 Likert scale items, comprising five items from the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8 (CSQ-8; Attkisson & Zwick, 2016) and an additional item to assess perceptions of symptom reduction.

text.text: Items on the CSQ are scored on a 4-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (low) to 4 (high), and the additional symptom reduction item was a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (low) to 5 (high).
Lastly, a clinician-administered treatment feedback interview was conducted to gather qualitative information on participants' perceptions to the treatment (Supplemental file 1).
Treatment drop-out, late cancellation, and no-show rates were used to characterize the feasibility of participant engagement.

Lastly, therapist adherence to the treatment protocol was assessed by the primary author (TH) using a checklist for each session; the protocol's feasibility was defined as the percentage deviation per session across all participants.
The Trauma History Questionnaire (THQ; Hooper et al., 2011) was administered during the study eligibility prescreen to assess for a criterion A index trauma.

text.text: The THQ is a 24-item questionnaire that participants could endorse = 'Yes' or deny = 'No' exposure to 24 potentially traumatic experiences.
The THQ was modified for the current study to evaluate for the presence of a criterion A traumatic experience (i.e., index trauma).
The PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5; Blevins et al., 2015) was used to assess past-month and past-week PTSD symptom severity during the intake and clinical trial, respectively.
text.formatted: The PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Blevins et al., 2015)</ref> was used to assess past-month and past-week PTSD symptom severity during the intake and clinical trial, respectively.

text.text: The PCL-5 is a 20-item self-report measure with each item corresponding to one of the PTSD symptoms from the DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

Items on the PCL-5 were anchored to participants' reported index trauma on the THQ and asked how much they are bothered by each symptom on a five-point Likert-type scale from0 = 'Not at all' to4 = 'Extremely.'
Items are summed to produce an overall score ranging from 0 to 80.
PCL-5 scores ≥ 31 were classified as a positive screen for probable PTSD during the prescreen (Blevins et al., 2015).

text.text: Brief Exposure Therapy.
Participants underwent eight sessions of twice-weekly BET, which primarily consisted of imaginal exposures and emotional processing similar to the PE protocol (Foa et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Participants underwent eight sessions of twice-weekly BET, which primarily consisted of imaginal exposures and emotional processing similar to the PE protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Foa et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Twice-weekly shorter-duration (45-min) exposure therapy sessions were used to improve acceptability for participants (Booysen & Kagee, 2021; Levinson et al., 2022; Sripada et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Twice-weekly shorter-duration (45-min) exposure therapy sessions were used to improve acceptability for participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Booysen & Kagee, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Levinson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Sripada et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Fewer and shorter sessions were also chosen, in part, to prevent ceiling effects that may have otherwise occurred with a full dose of PE.

That said, shorter duration exposure treatments are shown to be efficacious in treating PTSD (Booysen & Kagee, 2021; Cigrang et al., 2017), and shorter imaginal exposure sessions (60-min) have been shown to be noninferior to full-length (90-min) sessions (Nacasch et al., 2015; Minnen & Foa, 2006).

text.text: BET was administered by a master's level clinical psychology doctoral student (TH) with the consultation and supervision of licensed clinical psychologists (TA and SSZ) who have extensive experience in treating PTSD and conducting treatment outcome research.

The first BET session included psychoeducation about PTSD symptoms, rationale for imaginal exposures, treatment planning and goal setting, and the development of each participant's negative expectations related to undergoing the exposures (e.g., the exposure would cause them to break down and lose control).
For sessions two through seven, participants underwent imaginal exposures where they recounted their traumatic experience aloud in the present tense for 20 minutes.
Participants were asked to report pre-, post-, and peak subjective units of distress (SUDs) across all exposure sessions, a commonly used measure in exposure therapy (Wolpe & Lazarus, 1966).
text.formatted: Participants were asked to report pre-, post-, and peak subjective units of distress (SUDs) across all exposure sessions, a commonly used measure in exposure therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Wolpe & Lazarus, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: Before and after exposures, participants were asked to evaluate the likelihood of their negative expectations about the exposure to facilitate expectancy violations (Craske et al., 2008; Kooistra et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Before and after exposures, participants were asked to evaluate the likelihood of their negative expectations about the exposure to facilitate expectancy violations <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Craske et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kooistra et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Following each exposure, participants underwent 10-15 minutes of emotional processing, consisting of semi-structured questions targeting exposure mechanisms and unstructured, open-ended questions and reflections.

Instead of using out-of-session homework between exposures, participants were instructed to practice allowing themselves to experience thoughts, images, or feelings that arise between sessions, similarly to the instructions used in written exposure therapy (Sloan & Marx, 2019).
text.formatted: Instead of using out-of-session homework between exposures, participants were instructed to practice allowing themselves to experience thoughts, images, or feelings that arise between sessions, similarly to the instructions used in written exposure therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Sloan & Marx, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The last BET session covered treatment progress, next steps, referrals, if requested, as well as questionnaires assessing acceptability and providing feedback on treatment.

Following each imaginal exposure and emotional processing session, participants engaged in 20 minutes of moderate-intensity (70-75% MHR) exercise, with a 3-minute warm-up and a 2-minute cool-down, using a stationary bicycle and a heart rate monitor.
During the warm-up, participants had 3 minutes to reach the target heart rate.
Participants were instructed to adjust their heart rate to stay within their 70-75% MHR range.
During the exercise sessions, participants biked in silence and watched a video of a bike path.

Aligned with CONSORT and SCED recommendations, a combination of analytical approaches was used to analyze the acceptability and feasibility, treatment efficacy, and mechanism engagement of the BET and exercise protocol (Butcher et al., 2022; Kratochwill et al., 2026).

text.text: Data cleaning and statistical analyses were completed with R (v4.3.1; R Core Team, 2026).

Participants' perspectives on the BET and exercise protocol, participant engagement with treatment (i.e., cancellations, no-shows, dropouts), and therapists' adherence to the treatment protocol were evaluated to characterize acceptability and feasibility.

Visual analysis was used to explore changes in weekly self-reported PTSD symptom severity (i.e., PCL-5) and exposure therapy mechanisms (BEAQ, PTCI-9, and PANAS-NA) between baseline, treatment, and follow-up phases for each participant.

Visual analysis is regarded as a conservative method for SCED data since it relies on observing differences between phases, which often demand larger effects than statistical tests, and allows comparisons within and between subjects. (Kazdin, 2010; Lane & Gast, 2014).

text.text: Following their intake, participants completed the CEQ to assess the credibility and initial expectations of the BET and exercise protocol.

Most participants viewed the BET and exercise treatment as credible (M = 23 out of 36, range = 18-27) and expected the treatment to improve their symptoms at least somewhat (M = 18.3 out of 36, range = 14-26).

On the post-treatment satisfaction questionnaire, 50% of participants reported that the BET and exercise treatment was very difficult, while the other 50% reported that the treatment was moderately difficult.

Despite its difficulty, all participants (100%) reported that they would recommend BET and exercise to a friend, that it has helped their problems a great deal, and that the treatment has improved their problems much more than they originally thought it would.
Participants reported that the BET and exercise treatment met most of their needs (50%) or almost all of their needs (50%) for which they sought help.
Across all measures and time points, no significant adverse reactions or lasting symptom exacerbations occurred because of the BET and exercise protocol.
Participants provided qualitative feedback about the acceptability and feasibility of the BET and exercise treatment during the treatment feedback interview.

Themes from the interview included finding twice-weekly sessions helpful (P1, P5, P6; 50%), a positive experience of combining therapy and exercise (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6; 100%), that exercise after exposures helped regulate emotions and reduce dissociation (P1, P2, P6; 50%), and that exercising in silence helped facilitate independent reflection of the session (P1, P2, P4, P6; 66%).
Regarding negative feedback, participants reported that they wished the treatment were one to two weeks longer (P3, P5, P6; 50%) and could include more than one traumatic experience (P2 & P5; 33%).

text.text: The current study had a 0% attrition rate, 0% no-show rate, and 2% latecancellation/reschedule rate (i.e., one session).
All six participants who started treatment completed all of the twice weekly treatment sessions.

The current study maintained good fidelity to the treatment protocol, as 100.0% of individual study sessions demonstrated less than a 20% deviation from the protocol and 75.0% had perfect adherence (0% deviation).
Protocol adherence, averaged across all participants and sessions, was 97.9% (SD = 3.9%, range = 85.7%-100%).
All participants (6 of 6) displayed improvements in PTSD symptom severity level and/or slope between baseline and treatment phases (Figure 1).

text.text: Across 5 of 6 participants, sharp changes in PTSD symptom severity were observed during the third week of treatment; one participant displayed a notable decrease in scores during the fourth week of treatment.
The observed reductions in PTSD symptom severity were staggered across baseline lengths and occurred relative to the start of treatment, providing visual evidence of experimental control.
Participants displayed baseline stability in experiential avoidance, posttraumatic cognitions, and negative affect.

Participants displayed improvements in level and/or slope for experiential avoidance (4 of 6), posttraumatic cognitions (6 of 6), and negative affect (5 of 6) scores between baseline and treatment phases.

Participants' improvements in experiential avoidance (4 of 6), posttraumatic cognitions (6 of 6), and negative affect (5 of 6) continued or were maintained in the follow-up phase relative to the treatment phase.
The observed reductions in symptoms were staggered across baseline periods and occurred after treatment initiation, providing visual evidence of experimental control.
The Tau-U statistic was used to evaluate the percentage of overlap in scores across phases for each participant; a greater negative non-overlap indicated a larger within-case treatment effect.
Four participants (P1, P3, P4, and P6) exhibited large non-overlap (Tau-U Range = -.80 to -.100) for PTSD symptom severity scores between baseline and treatment phases.

Between treatment and follow-up phases, all participants displayed medium to large non-overlap (Tau-U Range = -.63 to -.100), indicating a continued reduction of PTSD symptoms following treatment for all participants.
All six participants showed 100% non-overlap (Tau-U = -1.00) in PTSD symptom severity scores between baseline and follow-up.
Medium to large treatment effects were also observed for experiential avoidance, posttraumatic cognitions, and negative affect for all participants (Table 2).

Between-case effect sizes indicate a large reduction in PTSD symptom severity scores from the baseline to treatment (Weighted Tau-U = -.79; HSP SMD = -0.91), treatment to follow-up (Weighted Tau-U = -.83; HSP SMD = -1.22), and from baseline to follow-up phases (weighted Tau-U = -1.00; HSP SMD = -1.23).

text.text: This pilot SCED study (n=6) used an open-label, staggered-baseline design to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, efficacy, and treatment-mechanism engagement of a twice-weekly PTSD treatment protocol that combines a mechanism-focused exposure therapy with moderate-intensity aerobic exercise.
Findings add to a growing body of literature evaluating the benefits of combining exposure-based treatments with aerobic exercise.
With implementation in mind, the current treatment protocol aimed to fit psychotherapy and exercise within a standard treatment session (≤60 minutes).

Results from the current study suggest that a treatment comprised only of 20-minute imaginal exposures and 10-15 minutes of processing combined with 25 minutes of exercise was sufficient to reduce PTSD symptoms and engage exposure therapy mechanisms in six consecutive patients.

The BET treatment approach adds to an emerging trend of abbreviated treatments for PTSD (e.g., brief imaginal exposure and PE-PC), suggesting that shorter duration treatments may be an appropriate approach to PTSD treatment (Sripada et al., 2022; Zoellner et al., 2023) and treatment augmentation research (Benito et al., 2025; McLean & Foa, 2024).
text.formatted: The BET treatment approach adds to an emerging trend of abbreviated treatments for PTSD (e.g., brief imaginal exposure and PE-PC), suggesting that shorter duration treatments may be an appropriate approach to PTSD treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Sripada et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Zoellner et al., 2023)</ref> and treatment augmentation research <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Benito et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">McLean & Foa, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: That said, two participants (33%) reported wanting treatment to be longer as they felt they benefited from the BET treatment and wanted to reduce their symptoms further.
A flexible-duration exposure treatment may be appropriate for higher-severity cases and those with multiple index traumas, as recommended in the PE protocol (Foa et al., 2007).

text.text: Despite this, all participants reported positive overall experiences with the treatment and indicated greater symptom reduction than they expected relative to past therapy experiences.

Almost all participants reported an increased desire to continue exercising after completing the BET and exercise treatment, which, if maintained, could have lasting physical and mental health benefits beyond PTSD symptoms (Villella & Villella, 2014; White et al., 2024).

text.text: Participants in the current study reported that exercising after exposures was helpful.

Prior research demonstrates that aerobic exercise can reduce sensitivity to physiological symptoms of anxiety (LeBouthillier et al., 2016), exert anxiolytic effects (Su et al., 2026), and improve emotion regulation (Wang et al., 2024).

text.text: Taken together, post-exposure exercise could strengthen the consolidation of safety learning while attenuating the emotional burden of imaginal exposures through anxiolytic and mood-regulating effects.

These latter interpretations are consistent with participants' subjective reports; several participants noted that exercise helped them regulate their emotions and process their exposure before leaving the sessions.

Future studies should examine how exercise could be used to regulate participants' emotions following exposures and characterize the degree to which self-directed reflection may influence safety learning.
Quantitative results of the current study should be interpreted with caution due to its small sample size and a relatively short baseline phase for some participants.
Nonetheless, preliminary results suggest the BET and exercise protocol produced large reductions in PTSD symptom severity.

Unlike prior exposure and exercise clinical trials, the current BET and exercise protocol included fewer treatment components to better target safety learning and memory processes (i.e., only imaginal exposures), was shorter in duration, and used a more restrictive and intensive exercise threshold (i.e., 70-75% MHR).

Alongside reductions in PTSD symptom severity, the BET and exercise protocol engaged putative mechanisms of exposure therapy as suggested in extant research (Hoffman et al., 2022; Kooistra et al., 2023; Y. Wang et al., 2024).

Visual inspection of exposure mechanisms indicates that one or more mechanism changed in tandem with their PTSD, suggesting the potential influence of more than one mechanism driving symptom change.

Future studies should examine the temporal influence of exposure mechanism scores in conjunction and independently of each other to examine if putative mechanisms affect distinct or synergistic effects on PTSD symptoms (Benito et al., 2025).

text.text: SCEDs are an emerging clinical trial methodology for pseudo-phase 1 or 2 clinical trials in psychotherapy research but come with several limitations.
The current pilot study did not include an active comparison group or a treatment-as-usual control.

Instead, treatment effects were examined for each participant relative to their own baseline; a staggered-baseline design with three-, four-, and five-week baselines was used to improve feasibility and reduce study attrition.

This approach does not, however, elucidate the extent to which exercise may improve safety learning and exposure therapy, how the BET and exercise protocol compares to other PTSD treatments, or how much change occurs between timepoints.

Despite efforts to standardize assessment timing relative to therapy sessions (i.e., the day before the first session of the week), only 12% of weekly assessments were completed before the first session of each week; though 100% were completed before the first session of the subsequent week.
As a result, analyses focused on changes relative to the week of the study and to study phases rather than on specific sessions during the treatment phase.
The current treatment protocol, study design, and adherence assessments were completed by the primary author (TH), which introduces bias into the study's results.
All participants from the current study were recruited following completion of another study investigating neural mechanisms in emotional learning and exercise in PTSD among adults exposed to IPV.
The shared pipeline was used to decrease the duration of study recruitment and improve feasibility.
This may have had positively biased participant views of BET and exercise due to their involvement in the prior study (Rosencrans et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This may have had positively biased participant views of BET and exercise due to their involvement in the prior study <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Rosencrans et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, The current study's sample of six participants is acceptable for an SCED study but is nonetheless underpowered for standard inferential tests.
The current sample was relatively homogenous and may not generalize to other populations as participants were all white females with IPV-related trauma.

Future studies should assess the efficacy of BET and exercise using more rigorous clinical trial methodologies (e.g., active control comparison, blinding, independent raters, diverse samples etc.) and representative samples of individuals with PTSD.

Results from the current study indicated that the treatment of PTSD symptoms with six sessions of brief imaginal exposure to traumatic memories following by moderate-intensity exercise was acceptable to participants, feasibly administered, and resulted in medium to large reductions of PTSD symptom severity all participants.

The current study highlights the potential clinical utility of a combined brief exposure and exercise treatment for PTSD and demonstrates a clear need for additional research about this and related treatment approaches.
Future studies should examine the additive effects of exercise on exposure therapy relative to active control, using larger, representative samples and rigorous clinical trial designs.
